name: Tara Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, thanks for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say gets passed on with your name. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I'm a junior buyer at a garden and hardware distributor that supplies about two hundred independent garden centres and hardware shops. I buy the seasonal stuff, so compost, bird feed, hose reels, and right now it's Christmas lights and de-icer. Most of my day is ringing suppliers and keeping the order sheet up to date, and I check the warehouse counts by walking the aisles with a clipboard.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, I know. Everyone else uses the scanner app, but I trust my own eyes more. My manager Graham lets me get away with it because I'm usually right about what's running low. I'm not quick with the new systems, I'll be honest.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Jonas, he's in his second year as an apprentice plumber, so money's a bit tight. We've got about two months of costs saved. My parents live forty minutes away and they've always said we can move back if we had to, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it was overblown, and leave it there. I don't really post online about this stuff. At work I'd say it to Graham over a coffee: see, the clipboard wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even the small stuff worries me. They keep talking about an automatic reorder system that reads the till data from the garden centres. That's half of what I do, and if it comes in even in a boring version, Graham might not need a second buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and try to make myself the person suppliers want to deal with. I'd try to get a bit better with the scanner app, because people keep saying I should. And we'd keep the two months saved and not spend on a holiday this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panicky, just that background feeling that I'm the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the automatic reorder system. Has anyone actually seen it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sales rep showed us the automatic reorder system in September. The system predicted the compost order better than I did for spring, which stung. Graham said it was clever but expensive, so maybe it doesn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday, then the takeaways on Fridays. Jonas's apprentice wage goes up next year, so we'd hang on until then. I'm not touching the savings for anything fun.

say: I'd say AI was **overblown** and leave it there, without posting online.
I'd joke with Graham that **the clipboard wins**.
think: The **automatic reorder** system could take half my job even in a boring version.
If it comes in, Graham might not need a **second buyer**.
do: Carry on and become the buyer **suppliers prefer** to deal with.
Try to get better with the **scanner app** colleagues keep recommending.
Keep the **two months** saved and skip a holiday this year.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a background sense of being **the slow one**.
S0.quote: The sales rep showed us the automatic reorder system in September. The system predicted the compost order better than I did for spring, which stung.
fieldNote: Even in AI Plateau, the **reorder system** threatens her routine screen work.
She leans on **gut feel** and walking the aisles, and distrusts apps.
Money is tight on Jonas's **apprentice wage**, which sharpens the worry.

steps.text: Keep ringing seasonal suppliers and walking the aisles with a clipboard
Practise with the warehouse scanner app colleagues already use
Skip this year's holiday and cut Friday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad for people like me but that's how business goes. I'm not one for blaming anybody, firms have to keep costs down or they close. I'd mostly keep my head down at work and do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm gone within a couple of years. If the system buys seasonal stock off till data, what's left is the big supplier deals, and my manager Graham does those. I'm the junior who doesn't even use the scanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at jobs in the warehouse or on the trade counter now, because those are hands-on and they'd last longer. I'd stop putting anything into the car fund and move it all to savings. And I'd talk to Jonas about whether we could manage on his wage plus a part-time job for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'd be sick about it but I'd try not to show it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Wouldn't learning the new system help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'm slow with it and they'd see that. The people who'll keep their jobs are the ones who are quick, like the girl in returns who already does everything on her phone. I'd rather go somewhere I'm good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them before Jonas, actually, because Mum would know straight away from my voice. She'd say come home, and I'd say no. But I'd keep that offer in my back pocket.

say: I'd say it's **sad but business**, because firms have to keep costs down.
I'd keep my **head down** at work and get on with the job.
think: I expect to be **gone within two years** once seasonal buying runs off till data.

do: Look for **warehouse or trade counter** jobs now, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Move the **car fund** into savings instead.
Work out with Jonas whether **his wage plus part-time** work covers the bills.
feel: **Alarmed** and sick about it, while hiding it at work.
S1.quote: If the system buys seasonal stock off till data, what's left is the big supplier deals, and my manager Graham does those.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, not just change it, which puts her at alarmed.
Her **centre view** means she blames no one, calling it business.
She'd rather move to **hands-on work** where she feels competent than fight the new system.

steps.text: Apply for warehouse or trade counter jobs at the distributor
Move the car fund into the emergency savings
Plan with Jonas to live on his wage plus part-time work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what anyone's supposed to do about something this fast. I'd probably say it a lot, actually, to anyone who asked. I'm not someone who'd march, but I'd vote for whoever had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job goes almost straight away, because it's all ordering and phone calls. The warehouse lasts until about 2031 when the robots come, so if I can get onto the floor I've got three years. After that I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham this month for a move to the warehouse, even at less money. We'd stop saving for the car and keep every spare bit. And honestly, we'd probably talk to my parents about moving back for a year to save rent while Jonas finishes his apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake every night, and Jonas would be too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jonas is a plumber. How does his work look in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than mine, because it's hands-on. Robots plumbing a house by 2031 feels far away to me, but you said it, so I'd believe it. He'd be the one keeping us going for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back with your parents. How would that actually feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful, a bit. I left home at nineteen and I swore I'd never go back. I'd rather move back with my parents than burn through the two months we've saved.

I wouldn't march, but I'd **vote** for whoever had a real plan.
think: My job is **ordering and phone calls**, so it goes almost straight away.
The **warehouse** lasts until about **2031**, giving me three years if I get on the floor.
do: Ask Graham **this month** for a warehouse job, even at lower pay.
Stop saving for the car and **keep every spare bit**.
Talk to my parents about **moving back** for a year to save rent.
feel: **Frightened**, lying awake every night alongside Jonas.
S2.quote: I left home at nineteen and I swore I'd never go back. I'd rather move back with my parents than burn through the two months we've saved.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as her only window, via the warehouse floor.
Jonas (her boyfriend, apprentice plumber) would become the **main earner**.
She has a plan, so not panicked, but expects her **income to go**.

steps.text: Ask Graham this month for a move to the warehouse floor
Stop the car fund and keep every spare bit in savings
Move back in with her parents for a year to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, let's see what the government does with them. I'd probably sound calmer than I felt. At work I'd say it's still a while off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I still think my job goes, just around 2031 instead of straight away. The difference is Jonas would be qualified by then, earning proper money. That changes a lot for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or so and watch what other distributors do, because I don't want to jump too early. Then I'd look for a warehouse supervisor role or a trade counter job. We'd keep saving, maybe get to four months by the time it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but more like a heavy feeling than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a year. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the big distributors actually sack buyers or just stop hiring them. If the big distributors just stop hiring buyers, I can hang on. If they start letting buyers go, I'd move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Graham, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, at first. Graham's nice but he's got his own job to worry about. I'd only tell him when I had something else lined up.

say: I'd say there are **a few years** and we'll see what the **government** does.
At work I'd say it's **still a while off**, sounding calmer than I feel.
think: My job still goes, around **2031** instead of straight away.
Jonas would be **qualified** by then, which changes a lot for us.
do: **Wait a year** and watch whether other distributors sack buyers or stop hiring.

feel: Still **worried**, more a **heavy feeling** than panic.
S3.quote: If the big distributors just stop hiring buyers, I can hang on. If they start letting buyers go, I'd move fast.
fieldNote: The five-year gap matters mainly because Jonas (her boyfriend) finishes his **apprenticeship**.

She still expects her **buying income** to end, so the mood stays alarmed.

steps.text: Watch for a year whether other distributors let buyers go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. I'd mean it, too. I don't believe half of what people say ten years out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I've got a good few years left as a buyer and I can get better at it. By 2036 Jonas has his own van, maybe, and we might have a kid. The robots in 2039 are a problem for future me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am and work on being good at the job, maybe finally learn the scanner properly. I'd keep saving a bit each month. And I'd keep an eye on the warehouse jobs, without jumping yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quietly. It's far enough off that I can mostly not think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said future you. What would you want her to have done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saved more, probably, and not stayed in a job just because it was comfortable. I know that about myself. I stay put too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd wait until Jonas has his own customers. A plumber with regulars is safer than a buyer with a clipboard. I'd want that sorted first.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and lots can change.
I'd admit I don't believe **forecasts** that far out.
think: I have a **good few years** as a buyer and can get better at it.
The **2039 robots** feel like a problem for future me.
do: Stay at the distributor and finally **learn the scanner** properly.
feel: **Anxious**, but quietly, since it's far enough off to ignore most days.
S4.quote: A plumber with regulars is safer than a buyer with a clipboard.
fieldNote: She knows she **stays put too long**, and says so.
Family plans hinge on Jonas (her boyfriend) building a **customer base**.
Ten years lets her **avoid thinking** about it, which she half admits is risky.

steps.text: Keep buying seasonal stock and learn the scanner app properly
Put a little into savings every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm slow with technology and I'd have no time to catch up. What would help is someone actually telling people like me where the jobs are, not an app, a person, and maybe help with rent while you switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the suppliers. The old suppliers I ring for bird feed have been in business forty years, and if nobody rings them anymore they'll miss it too. It's not just buyers who lose the conversation.

headlineQuote: The old suppliers I ring for bird feed have been in business forty years, and if nobody rings them anymore they'll miss it too.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old junior buyer** of seasonal garden and hardware stock, living with Jonas, an apprentice plumber.
She **avoids new technology**, trusts her clipboard, and knows she's the slow one with apps.
Her **centre view** means she blames no one; she calls it business and keeps her head down.
From **Steady Disruption** onwards she expects to lose her buying job and heads for the **warehouse floor**.
Longer warnings help mainly because Jonas finishes his trade and **becomes the steadier earner**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she's slow with technology and would have no time to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A **real person** pointing to where jobs are, plus **rent help** while switching.
